title: Effects of low-level prenatal lead exposure on child IQ at 4 and 8 years in a UK birth cohort study.
ehr_evidence: "The study sample was derived from the ALSPAC, a population-based study investigating environmental and genetic influences on the health, behaviour and development of children." Lead exposure was measured from whole blood samples analysed by inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (biospecimen assay), and IQ was measured at research clinics, not from electronic health records.
summary: A prospective UK birth cohort study (ALSPAC) examining the association between prenatal (first-trimester) blood lead concentrations and child IQ (verbal, performance, total) at 4 and 8 years.
key_findings: No association of prenatal blood lead with child IQ at 4 or 8 years in adjusted regression models (all p > 0.05).
No moderation effect of prenatal B-Pb on the association between child B-Pb and IQ at age 4 or 8 years (all p > 0.05).
In girls, positive association between prenatal B-Pb and IQ at 8 years: +0.71 verbal (p=0.021), +0.57 performance (p=0.099), +0.73 total IQ points per 1 mg/dl (p=0.017).
In boys, coefficients tended to be negative at 8 years: -0.15 verbal, -0.42 performance, -0.29 total IQ points per 1 mg/dl (all p > 0.200).
Maternal education was the strongest confounder, fully attenuating the crude associations in models 2 and 3.
No evidence for an effect of early-pregnancy maternal haemoglobin on the association between prenatal B-Pb and child IQ.
captured_features: Prenatal (first-trimester) maternal whole blood lead concentration (B-Pb)
Child verbal IQ, performance IQ and total IQ (WPPSI at 4 years, WISC-III at 8 years)
Maternal education, first-trimester smoking, first-trimester alcohol, maternal age, parity, time resident in Avon
Housing tenure, household crowding, family adversity index, weighted life events score
population: UK population-based birth cohort (ALSPAC); 4285 pregnant women with prenatal blood lead measured (delivery 1991-1992, Avon); offspring followed to IQ testing at 4 and 8 years.
limitations: Relatively small number of children with IQ measured at age 4 years and low numbers measured at both ages; particularly small sample in the moderation analysis.
IQ tests subject to error (child boredom, mood, tiredness, rapport with examiner).
Unable to adjust for maternal and paternal IQ, contributing to residual confounding.
Role of concomitant exposure to other pollutants (e.g., cadmium) not included.
Time lapse between exposure and outcome means unknown further childhood lead exposure was not accounted for.
